fetched_contents.text: Degradation by brown rot fungi increases the hygroscopicity of heat-treated wood Highlights * • Heat-treated and reference samples were degraded by brown rot fungi. * • Sorption isotherms were measured starting in desorption from the undried state. * • Brown rot degradation increased moisture content in desorption in all samples. * • Moisture content of heat-treated samples showed an increase also in absorption. * • Abstract Heat treatment increases the decay resistance of wood by decreasing its hygroscopicity, but the wood material remains degradable by fungi. This study investigated the degradation of heat-treated wood by brown rot fungi, with the aim of identifying fungal-induced hygroscopicity changes that facilitate degradation. Scots pine sapwood samples were modified under superheated steam at 200 and 230 °C and then exposed to Coniophora puteana and Rhodonia placenta in a stacked-sample decay test to produce samples in different stages of decay. Sorption isotherms were measured starting in desorption from the undried, decaying state to investigate their hygroscopic properties. Although there were substantial differences in degradative ability between the two fungi, the results revealed that decay by both species increased the hygroscopicity of wood in the decaying state, particularly at high relative humidity. The effect was stronger in the heat-treated samples, which showed a steep increase in moisture content at low decay mass losses. The reference samples showed decreased hygroscopicity in absorption from the dry state, while the heat-treated samples still showed an increase at low mass losses. Near infrared spectroscopy showed that the early stages of decay were characterised by the degradation of hemicellulose and chemical changes to cellulose and lignin, which may explain the increase in hygroscopicity. The results provide a new perspective on brown rot decay and offer insight into the degradation of heat-treated wood. Keywords Durability ; Dynamic vapor sorption ; Thermal modification ; Wood decay * Previous article * Next article 1. Introduction Heat treatment is a wood modification technique that relies on thermal degradation reactions to bring about changes in wood composition and properties. Of the wood cell wall polymers cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin, heat treatment has the strongest effect on the hemicellulose fraction, resulting in depolymerisation as well as dehydration and volatilisation of the resulting sugar units (Tjeerdsma et al., 1998; González-Peña et al., 2009). Lignin is also affected by heat treatment and undergoes cleavage as well as condensation reactions with itself and with carbohydrate degradation products (Tjeerdsma et al., 1998; Nuopponen et al., 2005; González-Peña et al., 2009). Crystalline cellulose is relatively resistant to thermal degradation, while amorphous cellulose shows behaviour similar to hemicellulose (González-Peña et al., 2009). The degradative changes caused by heat treatment change the hygroscopicity of the wood material (Hill et al., 2021). Wood is hygroscopic because the wood cell wall polymers all contain hydroxyl groups that attract water molecules, causing the absorption of moisture from the surrounding environment until an equilibrium state is achieved. Most of the hydroxyl groups accessible to water are found on the hemicelluloses, and as hemicelluloses are the most thermally labile cell wall polymer, heat treatment causes a reduction in the hygroscopicity of wood and reduces the amount of water that the wood can absorb at any given relative humidity (Hill et al., 2021). However, the reduction in hygroscopicity is not solely dependent on the loss of mass (Altgen et al., 2016, 2020), hemicellulose (Repellin and Guyonnet 2005) or accessible hydroxyl groups (Rautkari et al., 2013; Altgen et al., 2018). When the modification is carried out under dry conditions, heat treatment also causes other changes in the wood cell walls that further contribute to the reduction in hygroscopicity. Several explanations have been offered to explain the reduction in hygroscopicity, but none of them has been able to fully account for the behaviour of heat-treated wood (Hill et al., 2021). Heat treatment also improves the decay resistance of the wood material. Although the thermal degradation of the most easily digestible polymers in wood (hemicelluloses) can decrease the rate of fungal degradation, it is thought that the primary reason for the improved decay resistance of heat-treated wood is related to reduced hygroscopicity (Thybring 2013; Ringman et al., 2014, 2019; Zelinka et al., 2016). While the reasons for improved durability as a result of reduced moisture content are not fully understood, it is thought that the improvement is due to inhibited or reduced diffusion of fungal degradative agents into the wood cell wall (Thybring 2013; Ringman et al., 2014, 2019; Zelinka et al., 2016). Although heat treatment improves decay resistance, wood decaying fungi are still able to colonise the modified substrate and degrade it. Heat treatment appears to both delay the onset of wood degradation as measured by mass loss due to decay and reduce its rate after decay has begun (Ringman et al., 2016). It has also been shown that some wood decaying fungi are more efficient in degrading heat-treated wood than others, with the brown rot fungus Rhodonia placenta often emerging as the most efficient degrader (Kamdem et al., 2002; Welzbacher and Rapp 2007; Metsä-Kortelainen and Viitanen 2009; Chaouch et al., 2013). The eventual degradation of heat-treated wood and the differences in degradative ability between fungi suggest that the fungal degradative process may involve modification of the heat-treated wood that make it more amendable to further fungal degradation. fetched_contents.text: Prediction of the decay resistance of heat treated wood on the basis of its elemental composition Abstract The effect of heat treatment temperature on the elemental composition of Scots pine sapwood (Pinus sylvestris) has been investigated in the range of temperatures between 220 and 250 °C. The results revealed an important increase of carbon content, while oxygen content significantly decreases. Independently of the heat treatment temperature, elemental composition is strongly correlated with the mass losses due to thermal degradations. Carbon content as well as O/C ratio seem to represent valuable markers to estimate wood degradation after heat treatment. Heat treated specimens were exposed to fungal decay using the brown rot fungus Poria placenta and the weight losses due to fungal degradation were determined. Correlations between weight losses recorded after fungal exposure and elemental composition indicated that carbon content or O/C ratio can be used to predict wood durability conferred by heat treatment allowing us to envisage the development of a proper method to evaluate the quality of heat treated wood and predict its durability. These results also confirm that chemical modifications of wood cell wall polymers are the main factors responsible for wood durability improvement against fungal decay after heat treatment. Introduction Wood heat treatment is an attractive method to improve decay resistance of low natural durability wood species [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. During treatment, hemicelluloses and amorphous cellulose are strongly degraded, while lignin is believed to undergo thermo-crosslinking reactions [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14]. More recently, it has been shown that chemical modification of wood polysaccharides is the origin of the improvement of wood durability [15]. Due to the importance of dehydration reactions during heat treatment, we have investigated the changes of atomic O/C ratio as a potential marker to evaluate intensity of heat treatment using different methods like XPS [16] or microanalyses [17]. The results showed that elemental composition of heat treated wood could be a valuable marker to evaluate mass losses caused by thermo-degradation reactions and consequently treatment intensity. However, mass losses depend directly on heat treatment conditions and especially on heat treatment temperature, which can influence kinetics and selectivity of thermal degradation reactions. It seems therefore important to investigate the evolution of O/C ratio under different heat treatment conditions to check the correlations existing with mass losses and decay durability. The aim of this work was first to check the correlations between O/C ratio obtained for different heat treatment temperatures and mass losses due to the thermal degradation reactions before investigating, for a second time, the correlations with durability against fungal decay. fetched_contents.text: Use of wood elemental composition to predict heat treatment intensity and decay resistance of different softwood and hardwood species Abstract Heat treatment is an attractive alternative to improve decay resistance of low natural durability wood species. Decay resistance is strongly correlated to thermal degradations of wood cell wall components. Some recent studies proposed the use of wood elemental composition as a valuable marker to predict final properties of the material. These results, initially obtained with pine, have been extended to different softwood and hardwood species to check validity of the method using equipment specially designed to measure mass losses during thermal treatment. Heat treatment was performed on two softwood species (pine and silver fir) and three hardwood species (poplar, beech and ash) at 230 °C under nitrogen for different times to reach mass losses of 5, 10 and 15%. Heat-treated specimens were exposed to fungal decay using the brown rot fungus Poria placenta and the weight losses due to fungal degradation determined as well as initial wood elemental composition. Correlations between weight losses recorded after fungal exposure and elemental composition indicated that carbon content and O/C ratio can be used to predict wood durability conferred by heat treatment. Moreover, it was observed that for given curing conditions thermo-degradation patterns differed considerably according to the wood species. The sole analysis of wood physical properties like its density, thermal conductivity and diffusivity cannot allow explaining the observed differences, which should also depend on thermally activated chemical processes depending on wood chemical composition. Introduction The use of wood as building material is subject to increasing interest due to its intrinsic properties and its ability to fix carbon dioxide. Wood heat treatment by mild pyrolysis has been reported to improve some of its properties such as its biological durability and its dimensional stability. This process avoids the use of wood preservatives, constituting an attractive “non biocidal” alternative to classical preservation treatments. Indeed, even if heat treatment generates some volatile organic compounds and waste water having strong acidic and corrosive effect, it remains globally relatively safe for the environment. The influence of treatment conditions on chemical composition and conferred properties of heat-treated wood have therefore been intensively studied. Wood heat treatment induces chemical modifications of the main wood cell wall components. The lignin network is modified [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], the ratio between amorphous and crystalline cellulose is also changed [6], [7], [8], hemicelluloses are strongly degraded [7], [9] leading to formation of carbonaceous material within the wood [10]. These chemical modifications modify wood colour [11], [12], [13] and confer to the material new properties such as improved dimensional stability [14], [15], improved fungal resistance [16], [17], [18], lower affinity for water due to increase of wood surface hydrophobicity [18], [19], [20], [21], [22]. Different heat treatment conditions have been described in the literature [23], [24]. Among these, the wood torrefaction corresponds to heat treatment carried out at temperatures below 300 °C under inert gaseous atmospheres. Chemical reactions involved during torrefaction as well as final properties of the material depend strongly on the treatment temperature and of its duration. During torrefaction, wood is thermally decomposed at a slow rate [25]. Recently, it was reported that the anhydrous mass loss during the heat treatment could be a reliable and accurate marker to predict decay resistance of heat-treated wood [17], [26]. Hence, the control of the mass of the material during the heat treatment process will allow predicting its final durability. Due to the importance of dehydration reactions occurring during the heat treatment, the behaviour of carbon and oxygen contents has been evaluated through determination of wood’s elemental composition [27] and reactivity of free hydroxyl groups with acetic anhydride [4]. Indeed, previous studies have shown that heat treatment resulted in numerous dehydration reactions due to degradation of amorphous polysaccharides [6], [7], [8] jointly with the formation of carbonaceous materials within the wood structure leading to a strong decrease of wood’s O/C ratio [3], [10]. Moreover, dehydration reactions occurring during heat treatment have been reported to be at the origin of the lower reactivity of hydroxyl groups of wood cell wall polymers during acetylation [2], [4]. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the correlations between the improvement of the durability of different softwood and hardwood species and the mass losses induced by the heat treatment estimated on the basis of their O/C ratio. How mass loss measurements can be interpreted as decay resistance indicators

Mass loss measurements are commonly used in wood decay testing, but the evidence suggests they are best interpreted as part of a broader assessment rather than as a standalone indicator. The provided evidence includes mass-loss protocols used in decay testing, correlations between mass loss and fungal attack, and limitations of mass loss as a sole indicator.

The evidence shows that mass loss is measured during fungal decay testing. A study says that heat-treated specimens were exposed to fungal decay using the brown rot fungus Poria placenta and the weight losses due to fungal degradation were determined [N2-F2]. Another study reports that the mass loss of wood due to thermal modification can be measured, and in one case, the mass loss due to thermal modification was studied by measuring the weight of wood before and after thermal modification [N6-F4]. The same source also describes a correlation analysis between mass loss and equilibrium moisture content [N6-F4]. These examples indicate that mass loss is measured either during thermal treatment or during fungal decay exposure, and that the protocol typically involves weighing samples before and after the treatment or exposure [N2-F2][N6-F4].

Mass loss correlates with fungal attack and decay progression in several ways. First, the evidence shows that heat treatment delays the onset of wood degradation and reduces its rate after decay has begun [N1-F1]. This means that mass loss can be used to track when decay starts and how quickly it progresses. Second, the evidence states that the mass loss due to fungal degradation is determined after fungal exposure [N2-F2]. Third, the evidence says that the same mass loss can be obtained at shorter treatment duration with higher temperature or by using longer treatment time with lower temperature [N2-F2]. This implies that mass loss is not a fixed indicator of treatment severity but depends on the combination of temperature and time. Finally, the evidence notes that mass loss is strongly correlated with treatment intensity and with wood decay resistance [N2-F2]. In other words, mass loss can be used to estimate how much degradation has occurred and how durable the wood is likely to be.

Despite these correlations, mass loss has important limitations as a standalone indicator. The evidence explicitly states that the reduction in hygroscopicity is not solely dependent on mass loss, hemicellulose, or accessible hydroxyl groups [N1-F1]. Another source says that mass loss does not detect the early stages of decay well [N3-R2]. The evidence also notes that wood decaying fungi can still colonize the modified substrate and degrade it, so mass loss does not eliminate the possibility of decay [N1-F1]. A further source says that some fungi are more efficient in degrading heat-treated wood than others, with the brown rot fungus Rhodonia placenta often emerging as the most efficient degrader [N1-F1]. These findings show that mass loss can be influenced by fungal species and treatment history, and that it may not fully capture the biological complexity of decay resistance.

The evidence also highlights that mass loss is not sufficient to explain all changes in wood properties. The evidence says that the sole analysis of wood physical properties like density, thermal conductivity, and diffusivity cannot explain the observed differences, which should also depend on thermally activated chemical processes depending on wood chemical composition [N2-F2]. In the same study, the authors note that treatment intensity estimated from mass losses due to thermal degradation depends on treatment duration and temperature [N2-F2]. This means that mass loss alone may not distinguish between thermally equivalent samples with different chemical modifications and different decay resistance outcomes.

Taken together, the evidence supports the interpretation that mass loss can be used as a decay-resistance indicator, but only when paired with other information. It is useful for tracking fungal attack, estimating treatment severity, and predicting durability because mass loss is strongly correlated with treatment intensity and decay resistance [N2-F2][N6-F4]. However, it should not be used as a standalone indicator because it is influenced by treatment conditions, fungal species, and chemical processes that are not fully captured by mass loss alone [N1-F1][N3-R2][N2-F2]. In practical terms, mass loss is best viewed as part of a multi-variable assessment that includes elemental composition, equilibrium moisture content, fungal attack, and treatment history [N6-F4][N2-F2].

What wood composition changes predict decay resistance after heat treatment

Heat treatment alters wood composition by degrading or modifying the main cell-wall components, especially hemicellulose, amorphous cellulose, and lignin. The evidence shows that thermal treatment has the strongest effect on hemicellulose, causing depolymerisation, dehydration, and volatilisation of the resulting sugar units [N1-F1]. Lignin is also affected by heat treatment and undergoes cleavage as well as condensation reactions with itself and carbohydrate degradation products [N1-F1]. Crystalline cellulose is relatively resistant to thermal degradation, while amorphous cellulose shows behaviour similar to hemicellulose [N1-F1]. This means that hemicellulose is the most thermally labile component, and its degradation reduces the wood’s hygroscopicity and may also reduce the availability of easily degradable substrates for fungi [N1-F1].

Extractives are also implicated in thermal modification. The evidence says that during heat treatment, extractives evaporate or polymerize [N1-R2]. This matters because extractives are often a source of nutrients or labile compounds that fungi can use for growth and decay, so their reduction can improve decay resistance by limiting fungal access to degradable material [N1-R2]. The evidence also notes that, after heat treatment, the hemicelluloses display reduced chain mobility when moisture is present and that their removal reduces this property in thermally treated wood [N1-R3]. That same evidence further states that cellulose, hemicelluloses, and lignin are the main structural elements of wood and that heat treatment involves degradation of these components to different levels [N1-R4]. So, the main compositional changes are not limited to one component but affect the cell-wall polymer system broadly.

Cellulose itself is important because the evidence says that cellulose, hemicelluloses, and lignin are the main structural elements of wood and that heat treatment involves degradation of these components to different levels [N1-R4]. It also says that thermal modification alters the chemical composition of wood and makes it less vulnerable to insects, rot, and decay [N7-R3]. The decay-resistance explanation in the evidence is tied to reduced hygroscopicity and to the removal or blocking of susceptible hydroxyl groups [N5-R5]. Because wood is hygroscopic, the hydroxyl groups on hemicelluloses are especially important for moisture attraction, and heat treatment reduces hygroscopicity by reducing the accessible hydroxyl groups and by other cell-wall changes [N1-F1]. That same evidence explains that the reduction in hygroscopicity is not solely dependent on mass loss, hemicellulose, or accessible hydroxyl groups [N1-F1]. So, cellulose and lignin changes are not just passive effects of thermal modification; they contribute to the overall structural and hydrophobic state of the wood.

The evidence also emphasizes that thermal modification reduces hygroscopicity and increases decay resistance. The direct statement is that “heat treatment increases the decay resistance of wood by decreasing its hygroscopicity” [N1-F1]. Another source says that the main reason for improved decay resistance is related to reduced moisture content and inhibited or reduced diffusion of fungal degradative agents into the wood cell wall [N1-F1]. A further source adds that heat treatment improves decay resistance, but fungi can still colonize the modified substrate and degrade it [N1-F1]. This is important because it shows that thermal modification does not eliminate decay resistance entirely; it delays the onset of decay and reduces its rate after decay has begun [N1-F1]. The result is that the wood becomes more durable, but it is not immune to fungal attack.

Taken together, the composition changes that predict decay resistance after heat treatment are:
- degradation of hemicellulose [N1-F1][N1-R2],
- degradation of amorphous cellulose [N1-F1],
- lignin modification and condensation reactions [N1-F1],
- polymerization or evaporation of extractives [N1-R2],
- reduction in accessible hydroxyl groups and reduced hygroscopicity [N1-F1],
- reduced moisture content and inhibited diffusion of fungal degradative agents [N1-F1],
- altered cellulose and lignin content and structure [N1-R4][N7-R3].

These changes collectively improve decay resistance by making the wood less attractive to fungi, less hygroscopic, and less prone to rapid decay progression [N1-F1][N5-R5]. The evidence therefore supports a model in which heat-treated wood durability is explained by a combination of chemical degradation, hydrophobicity changes, and structural modifications rather than by a single component alone [N1-F1][N7-R3].

How elemental composition can be interpreted as a proxy for thermal treatment and decay resistance

Elemental composition changes during thermal modification are consistent with thermal degradation. The evidence shows that carbon content increases and oxygen content decreases during heat treatment, with the O/C ratio serving as a valuable marker [N2-F2]. Another source reports that oxygen content decreases with treatment intensity and is directly proportional to treatment time, while carbon content increases significantly [N8-R1]. A third source states that O/C ratios of wood surfaces are reduced after thermo-vacuum and superheated steam heat treatments, indicating thermal degradation [N8-R2]. These findings support the interpretation that elemental composition is not just a passive record of mass loss but a direct indicator of thermal degradation intensity [N2-F2][N8-R1][N8-R2].

Carbon and oxygen are the most important elements for thermal-degradation interpretation because they are strongly linked to dehydration and thermally driven chemical changes. The evidence says that during heat treatment, dehydration reactions occur and that previous studies have shown that heat treatment results in numerous dehydration reactions due to degradation of amorphous polysaccharides, jointly with formation of carbonaceous materials within the wood structure [N2-F2]. These reactions strongly decrease the O/C ratio [N2-F2]. The same source also says that the anhydrous mass loss during heat treatment can be a reliable and accurate marker to predict decay resistance of heat-treated wood [N2-F2]. This implies that elemental composition, especially the O/C ratio, can be used to infer both the extent of thermal degradation and the likely durability consequences of that degradation.

Nitrogen and other elements are less directly emphasized in the provided evidence, but they are still relevant as part of the broader elemental profile. The evidence does not provide a detailed breakdown of nitrogen content across treatment conditions, so it cannot be used to make a strong general claim about nitrogen alone [N2-R1][N2-R3]. ## 1) What wood composition changes predict decay resistance after heat treatment?

The branch report on composition changes shows that thermal modification mainly affects the main cell-wall polymers: hemicellulose is the most thermally labile component, and its degradation is a major factor in improved decay resistance [N1-F1]. Amorphous cellulose is also degraded, while crystalline cellulose is relatively resistant to thermal degradation [N1-F1]. Lignin is modified by heat treatment, undergoing cleavage and condensation reactions [N1-F1]. Extractives are also affected, with evidence that they evaporate or polymerize during treatment [N1-R2]. This means that decay resistance is not just about one component; it arises from a combination of changes in hemicellulose, cellulose, lignin, extractives, and the overall cell-wall structure [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N7-R3].

The branch report also emphasizes that thermal treatment reduces hygroscopicity and increases decay resistance. The direct statement is that “heat treatment increases the decay resistance of wood by decreasing its hygroscopicity” [N1-F1]. Another explanation says that improved decay resistance is related to reduced moisture content and inhibited or reduced diffusion of fungal degradative agents into the wood cell wall [N1-F1]. This is important because hygroscopicity is central to fungal attack: the more moisture a wood can absorb, the easier it is for fungi to colonize and degrade it [N1-F1][N5-R5]. So, the composition changes that matter are those that reduce water absorption, make the wood less attractive to fungi, and alter the cell-wall chemistry that fungi exploit.

The branch report on elemental composition shows that carbon content increases and oxygen content decreases during heat treatment, with the O/C ratio being a valuable marker [N2-F2]. A third source says that O/C ratios of wood surfaces are reduced after thermo-vacuum and superheated steam heat treatments, indicating thermal degradation [N8-R2]. These findings support the idea that elemental composition is not just a passive record of mass loss but a direct indicator of thermal degradation intensity [N2-F2][N8-R1][N8-R2].

Carbon and oxygen are the most informative elements for thermal-degradation interpretation because they are strongly linked to dehydration and thermally driven chemical changes.
